blocks.text: Chapter 4.
[Pafogai](/ˈpɑfOɡI/) [Du](/ˈdu/), [Dzego](/ˈdzɛɡO/). 3724, Snowmoon 24.

[Fin](/ˈfɪn/) and [Zei](/ˈzA/) were sitting at a table in an outdoor courtyard. Some of the nearby tables were empty, and at other tables they could see a few groups of teenagers and a few older couples sitting and eating.

Through the opening at the entrance, [Fin](/ˈfɪn/) could see across the street a teenager climbing up a wooden ladder that had been put up hastily against a public lamp post. Very soon, he was already at the top, and he immediately got to work unscrewing a security camera. Once he finished, he put the camera into a black pouch, and then climbed back down.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) tapped his hand on the table. [Fin](/ˈfɪn/)'s eyes snapped back, and he once again started looking intently at an animation on [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s hand device.

The animation plays on a grid of black and white squares. Small gliders fly in from the right toward a dotted vertical wall. Near the bottom the wall holds, but near the top it breaks open, and scattered debris spills through into the territory on the left. A turn counter ticks up in the corner.
"Okay, so what am I seeing here?", [Fin](/ˈfɪn/) asked.

"This was from my last [Minpentai](/ˈmɪnpɛntI/) game. We were playing with the 'rotate one eighty if three' rule. Someone discovered this new way to breach the usual wall construction, and flooded their opponent's territory with garbage. I'm trying to figure out some countermeasures."
"What's the endgame? Are you trying to get to a perfect wall, or is it rock paper scissors all the way down?"
"Well, remember, the rules are time-reversible. So any wall that can be created in some way can be destroyed in some way."
"Huh?"

"Remember when we were still in middle school, and we thought that in those movies the good guys or the bad guys or whoever were stupid for putting the shield generator outside of the shield so the other side could find it and destroy it?"
"Yeah."

"Turns out they weren't dumb, we are. Because the laws of physics are time-reversible, nothing can be invincible. Anything that can be created can be destroyed. You just have to take the path that creates it and do the same thing in reverse. So a shield that can't be destroyed is not something that can be created. There has to be a weakness somewhere — it's just a matter of how well you hide it."
"Are you trying to get into defense or something?"
"Hey, I'm just trying to win the championship. This year is the last year I can participate, and if I win, go to the nationals."
"You mean this year is your last chance to impress [Bai](/ˈbI/)?"
"Hey-"
A robot slid up to them.

"[jie](/ˈʤjɛ/) [mo](/ˈmO/) [kai](/ˈkI/) [tu](/ˈtu/) [jie](/ˈʤjɛ/) [hei](/ˈhA/) [ja](/ˈʤɑ/) [ma](/ˈmɑ/)?", it asked in the classic deliberately cute [Dzegoban](/ˈdzɛɡObɑn/) typical of restaurant robots. "Do you want to eat or drink?"
[Fin](/ˈfɪn/) looked at the screen on the robot.
The robot's screen shows four picture buttons: a cup labelled [ja](/ˈʤɑ/), a leaf labelled [kai](/ˈkI/), a horned animal's face labelled [bau](/ˈbW/), and a fish labelled [lui](/ˈlwi/).
He clicked on "kai", and then on a picture of a salad.

The next screen shows a salad bowl in the middle, labelled [kai](/ˈkI/) [can](/ˈtsɑn/), with arrows pointing into it from five ingredients: lettuce, labelled [dze](/ˈdzɛ/) [liu](/ˈlju/); a bottle of olive oil, [lei](/ˈlA/) [kai](/ˈkI/) [fun](/ˈfun/); a handful of nuts, [gai](/ˈɡI/) [lie](/ˈljɛ/); a tomato, [jau](/ˈʤW/) [jin](/ˈʤɪn/) [lie](/ˈljɛ/); and an avocado, [jia](/ˈʤjɑ/) [dzu](/ˈdzu/) [lie](/ˈljɛ/).
[Fin](/ˈfɪn/) clicked again, and then clicked a few more buttons to order tea. The robot beeped in acknowledgement, and then slid over to get closer to [Zei](/ˈzA/).
"Wow, everything is getting so picture-based now!"
"Well my last DU class was in linguistics so finally I get to be the genius here."

[Fin](/ˈfɪn/) took a small paper booklet out of his backpack. On the front cover, there was the [Bansunpei](/ˈbɑnsunpA/) logo: two horizontal arms, one from the left and one from the right, meeting in the middle to hold their hands. Above the logo was the title: "[po](/ˈpO/) [so](/ˈsO/) [dze](/ˈdzɛ/) [go](/ˈɡO/) [ban](/ˈbɑn/) [de](/ˈdɛ/) [sia](/ˈsjɑ/)" — "the conception of [Dzegoban](/ˈdzɛɡObɑn/) version nine".
"Tell me more?"

"You know how after we got the number of roots down to 256, the word was that we're going to keep going, and soon enough express everything through the four cardinal elements — earth, air, fire and water?"
"Yeah?"
"Turns out the [Bansunpei](/ˈbɑnsunpA/) wants to give up on that now. Stick to 256, and push the next version of [Dzegoban](/ˈdzɛɡObɑn/) in a different direction."
"And what's that?"
"Go visual. So first of all, they're actually seriously thinking of bringing back hieroglyphics."
"What?"

"Switching to the Veridian alphabet made sense back then because all the old symbols were hard to draw. But now we have computers. The problem isn't output, it's input. And the trick is, they're figuring out new symbols where some parts of the symbol encode the whole pronunciation, so you can look at the symbol and know exactly how it's pronounced if you forgot. And the rest of the symbol still tries to cover the meaning."
"Okay...?"

"There's a bigger change in how they are thinking. Language so far has been very one-dimensional, because speech is one-dimensional, you're saying one word after the other, and you write what you speak. But if you think about parts of 'language' that are not tied to speech, say, you like math — so think of the quadratic formula."
"Minus b plus minus square root of b squared minus four a c all over two a?"

"Think how ugly that looks if you had to write it down and show it to someone on a screen. Like, imagine someone reading those words on a screen right now and how that must make them feel. Now think of the equation, the way we normally write it down. I still don't remember the whole thing, but I remember it looks nice! It's a pretty picture. The fraction line splits things into top and bottom, there's a root, and it's easy to see what's inside the root and what's outside."
"So they want to make all of written [Dzegoban](/ˈdzɛɡObɑn/) like that?"
"Yep."

"You know, there's an old result: if you take the same text, and translate it into every language, the lengths of the translations are different. But if you take the translations, and compress them — literally, any off-the-shelf compression used in any of your compute devices — the lengths end up almost the same. So it's all the same amount of information. The question is always: how do you organize it so that it's the most accessible and useful?"
[Zei](/ˈzA/) pondered for a moment, thinking back to the thermodynamics lecture from a month ago. Information is information, the only question is how to arrange it. [Zei](/ˈzA/) nodded.

"So that's what the [Bansunpei](/ˈbɑnsunpA/) is A/B testing right now all across [Dzego](/ˈdzɛɡO/). Altogether, the priests came up with six different styles of visualization, and they're giving out reputation points if you adjust any of your writing or signs to their new ideas or report on your experiences reading things put up by others."
"Wait ... they're doing that level of nationwide organizing, all just to optimize our language yet again?"
"I guess so..."

[Zei](/ˈzA/) walked toward the half-kilometer-tall pyramid — the most visible landmark at the southern edge of [Pafogai](/ˈpɑfOɡI/) [Du](/ˈdu/). From the outside, it looked like a smooth clad stone pyramid with a square base, like something that had been built by a great civilization a thousand years ago. Interrupting the stone were two rows of trees along a path, starting from the position where [Zei](/ˈzA/) was standing ane leading to a point halfway to the top, and another row of trees going horizontally around the pyramid at exactly the halfway height.

But the looks were deceptive. Building a pyramid that tall would be far too expensive, even for Veridia, or even the Arctics. This was a pre-existing mountain with pre-existing caves, which was refurbished to look like a pyramid, with the caves converted into living and working spaces. A portion of the [Dzego](/ˈdzɛɡO/) government was located there, along with many major businesses — though space was expensive.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) stopped at a streetlight, and crossed [Dzai](/ˈdzI/) [Gun](/ˈɡun/) street: the last street before [Pafogai](/ˈpɑfOɡI/) [Du](/ˈdu/) officially ended, and the point at which a straight well-maintained path leading directly to the entrance of the mountain pyramid began.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) opened and closed each finger on his injured arm, then repeatedly spread out his fingers and put them back together. He simulated some button pressing motions. His arm felt fully healed, though [Zei](/ˈzA/) knew that his reaction time would still be a little bit slower.

The street curved up with about a ten percent slope, roughly doubling [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s calorie consumption as he walked along it. And [Zei](/ˈzA/) could feel it. His mind subconsciously stopped running through strategies for the upcoming match, and switched to simply marveling at the beauty of the pyramid.

When [Zei](/ˈzA/) was somewhat further up, he briefly looked back, and marveled at the view of [Pafogai](/ˈpɑfOɡI/) [Du](/ˈdu/): a sprawling series of low-rise buildings interspersed with trees, the flickering lights of various small shops and factories producing and selling all kinds of goods, all inside a perfectly regular grid of streets — seventeen streets two hundred meters apart from north to south, and thirty three streets one hundred meters apart from east to west. Some of the roads snaked between being fully above ground when they could afford to, and the portion for cars going below ground when the sidewalks needed the whole space to accommodate pedestrians.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) turned forward again, and kept climbing. About five minutes later, he arrived at the main door.
[Zei](/ˈzA/)'s watch buzzed.
A message from [Fin](/ˈfɪn/): [jie](/ˈʤjɛ/) [fe](/ˈfɛ/) [hen](/ˈhɛn/) [dzi](/ˈdzi/).
"Wish you luck", [Fin](/ˈfɪn/) had messaged him.

As instructed by some signs on the side of the main door, [Zei](/ˈzA/) turned left, walked about thirty meters along the horizontal path covered with trees, and entered the mountain pyramid through a smaller side entrance.

On the inside, the tunnels looked like the corridors that one might see inside a modern building. Each corridor was about two meters wide, and three meters tall; the lower two meters were a rectangle, and the upper meter a semicircle. The stone was polished clean, and looked like the interior of any other well-maintained building, though without the windows. Occasionally, [Zei](/ˈzA/) would pass by rooms with open doors. He could not tell which tunnels, and which rooms, were refurbished caves and which were dug out from scratch.
He followed the signs, turning right and down, then left, then straight and down for about a hundred meters. Finally, another right turn.

After about ten meters, he saw the door. On the sides, a series of stone bricks, curving near the top into an arch. At the center of the top, there was a symbol: two horizontal arms, meeting in the middle with clashing fists.
He walked in. An older woman noticed him and turned to him.
"Oh hi, [Zei](/ˈzA/)!"
"Ah, [Mu](/ˈmu/), good to see you again!"
"Excited for the quarter finals?"
"Yep!"
"Well be careful. Remember, you're going to be part of a team now. You're a math guy, not a diplomat. You didn't even remember my birthday!"
"Hey, the teams are randomly assigned! No relationships to manage, it's more like math than diplomacy."
"You'd be surprised. I think it makes the real-time diplomacy all the more important."
Another woman walked in, about the same age as [Zei](/ˈzA/).
"Ah, [Zei](/ˈzA/), we meet again."
[Zei](/ˈzA/)'s facial expression immediately turned into a frown. [Bai](/ˈbI/) had beaten him three out of three times over the past years, and was hardly magnanimous in victory. He turned away.

[Bai](/ˈbI/) walked up closer, and put her hand on [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s shoulder. "So, you afraid of me, [Zei](/ˈzA/)? You know I enjoy making you feel afraid. Taking your excitement about getting some prize money to buy a compute box for your mom, and snatching it all away, getting myself a vacation in the beautiful south islands of Redshire. I should send you pictures."
[Zei](/ˈzA/) clenched his fists.
"See you in battle! Or maybe you'll lose to someone else this round before you even get to a game against me." She laughed, and slowly walked away.
A bell buzzed. A robotic voice, more stern than the coffee shop robots, instructed all players to get to their stations.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) walked into one of the elevator pods on the wall. The door closed, and he could feel the elevator start to descend. A tray opened up, and a robotic voice, this time cute like the robots bringing food and drinks, asked [Zei](/ˈzA/) for all electronic devices. [Zei](/ˈzA/) took out his hand device, took off his watch, and put both on the tray. The tray retreated back into the side of the elevator.
A quarter minute later, the elevator door opened, exposing a giant room with over a thousand people watching. A path lit up, showing the way to a giant game console with a chair.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) gazed in awe at the room. This was [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s first time there — the games before the quarter-finals had been played in much humbler circumstances. He stared, amazed that a high-school programming game was able to secure this kind of space. Then his mind snapped back — he would ask [Mu](/ˈmu/) about it later, he thought. Right now, he wasn't there to enjoy, he was there to compete and win.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) walked forward. He could make out the silhouettes of three other players walking forward in the distance, but it was too dark to see who they were. He got to the chair, and sat down.

Drones about the size of a hand device buzzed as they flew around [Zei](/ˈzA/), scanning for any kind of equipment that could be used for cheating. If [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s hand device or watch had been with him, they would have automatically done the same in reverse — demand and verify an attestation from the manufacturer and two inspectors that the drone's firmware was running an anti-cheat scan and was not there to kill him. But here, [Zei](/ˈzA/) was without his electronic support, and so he had to rely on trust.

Half a minute later, the drones were satisfied, and flew away. A tray slid out from under the game console, offering glasses attached to a long cable. [Zei](/ˈzA/) picked up the glasses. He slid them under and behind his arm, so that the cable would rest behind him, and then put the glasses on.
A loud automated voice, once again stern, announced: "[MU](/ˈmu/) [GU](/ˈɡu/) [GEI](/ˈɡA/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)". Starting in fifty ticks.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) calmed down and tried to put his stress behind him, and rehearsed once again in his head the tactics. Walls, gliders, rocks, techniques for extracting usable negentropy from rocks, sideways attacks. Though every game there's always some kind of new rule, and the most important tactic of all was knowing how to adapt.
"[LE](/ˈlɛ/) [MU](/ˈmu/) [GEI](/ˈɡA/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)". Starting in twenty-five ticks.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) closed his eyes briefly, and breathed.
"[PA](/ˈpɑ/) [GU](/ˈɡu/) [GEI](/ˈɡA/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)"

"Welcome to the first quarter-final round of the eighteenth year of the [Minpentai](/ˈmɪnpɛntI/) tournaments. Tonight, four games will be taking place, one after the other. By midnight, we will know who is advancing to the semi-finals, and who will have to find another career. Or try harder for next year!"
"Today, fated by chance to be on team [Ja](/ˈʤɑ/), we have [Pan](/ˈpɑn/) [Munbau](/ˈmunbW/) and [Dza](/ˈdzɑ/) [Dzingo](/ˈdzɪnɡO/)."
"And on team [Zau](/ˈzW/), we have ... [Zei](/ˈzA/) [Leimin](/ˈlAmɪn/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/) [Jahen](/ˈʤɑhɛn/)."
[Zei](/ˈzA/) froze.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) could see the game field, which at the beginning appeared completely black. He saw in the corner of his display his symbol: a pattern of dots that, were a copy of it anywhere on the board, would allow him to see everything within thirty squares.

He drew a few copies of his symbol in the bottom right corner of the board, where he was allowed to put down squares during the initiation phase. As soon as he did, nearby parts of the game field became visible. Almost simultaneously, he also became able to see a few parts of the field at the bottom left. [Bai](/ˈbI/) had put down her symbols too.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) saw [Bai](/ˈbI/) setting up walls and glider factories — gliders that would fly right to a nearby rock formation, and then reflect one glider back into [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s territory where a mirror wall would send the glider right back, but also shoot another glider upward.
He began to do the same. He experimented with a few glider and wall formations in his sandbox, and after confirming that they work, deployed them to the field.
"[MU](/ˈmu/) [GU](/ˈɡu/) [GEI](/ˈɡA/) [TAU](/ˈtW/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)"
The battle begins in fifty ticks.

Normally, at this stage, the players would be speaking intensely by voice chat, coordinating their strategies. Between [Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/), neither spoke a word. The closest there was to communication was [Zei](/ˈzA/) intentionally not targeting gliders toward a few rock formations, [Bai](/ˈbI/) taking the hint and taking those rock formations herself, and similarly leaving some rock formations to [Zei](/ˈzA/).
"[LE](/ˈlɛ/) [MU](/ˈmu/) [GEI](/ˈɡA/) [TAU](/ˈtW/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)"
Twenty-five ticks.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) suddenly realized: there had not yet been a new rule announced. The rules were the same that he had played many times before. Would the rule be announced at the start? Or was something else going on?
No time for speculating, [Zei](/ˈzA/) thought. Have to focus on the game.
"[PA](/ˈpɑ/) [GU](/ˈɡu/) [SO](/ˈsO/) [BI](/ˈbi/) [ZE](/ˈzɛ/) [HA](/ˈhɑ/) [MU](/ˈmu/) [FO](/ˈfO/) [SHI](/ˈʃi/) [LE](/ˈlɛ/) [PA](/ˈpɑ/) ..."
"[TAU](/ˈtW/) [FA](/ˈfɑ/)"
Gliders started flying.
Larger spaceships flew out from [Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s bases.

For the first few hundred turns, there was no combat — it was simply a matter of expanding into the field and gathering resources. Gliders flew out, interacted with rock formations, and created more gliders. Spaceships flew out, acting as large slow-moving gliders that eventually crashed into a rock formation in a controlled way, leaving behind copies of each player's symbols. The portion of the game field that [Zei](/ˈzA/) could see increased.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s territories reached each other. A few stray gliders from [Bai](/ˈbI/) accidentally flew into [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s territory, and wrecked one of his factories. [Zei](/ˈzA/) cursed silently, and spent his next intervention turn putting up more walls facing [Bai](/ˈbI/). When putting up one of his walls, his finger slipped, and he accidentally created a glider that began to fly back toward his own base. [Zei](/ˈzA/) cursed silently, but then felt a sigh of relief when the glider harmlessly crashed into a rock formation.

A thousand turns later, the two sides' gliders and ships met. At the same time, the first intervention turn came. Here, all players were able to put down more squares near any copy of their symbols. [Zei](/ˈzA/) frantically adjusted his forces to more effectively attack Dza.

At the front, [Zei](/ˈzA/) put down a "moving wall" design that he had perfected — a sort of large glider that flew half as fast, but was optimized for reflecting more basic types of gliders right back at the sender. Right behind his three moving walls, all aimed at Dza's corner of the game board, he put his symbol-carrying spaceships.

On [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s side, her gliders and Pan's flew into each other's territories with roughly equal frequency. [Bai](/ˈbI/) had some success in sending gliders deep inside Pan's territory, turning some rock formations into a chaotic mess that blasted gliders everywhere, and destroyed some of Pan's symbols. Pan, meanwhile, was more effective at pushing into the center, and then rotating back, attacking some of [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s formations from behind.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) then rolled out his next move: sending three unusual-looking gliders deep into Dza's territory along the edge. The gliders hit the wall that Dza had set up around his home base in the northeast corner, and came together into [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s symbol for exactly one turn — [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s next intervention turn. [Zei](/ˈzA/) quickly removed junk and put up walls around the symbol, and three gliders aimed in strategic directions. He now had a base right at the core of Dza's territory.

The audience was able to see a large detailed map of everything that was happening onscreen. [Fin](/ˈfɪn/), checking from far away on his hand device, saw the summary view which showed the locations of each player's symbols:

The summary map shows four kinds of marks. Dza's plus signs cluster in the northeast corner. [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s circles run up the eastern side from his base in the bottom right, with one reaching right into the northeast corner. Pan's triangles are spread across the north, west and center, and [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s squares are gathered in the bottom left.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) continued attacking Dza. Remove one of the two players completely, he thought, and that takes out half the activity in the intervention turns — always the biggest source of surprise.
Meanwhile, more of [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s symbols disappeared, as Pan launched an attack going into the middle of the bottom of the field, seeking to cut [Zei](/ˈzA/) off from [Bai](/ˈbI/).

Watching from the sidelines, [Mu](/ˈmu/) sighed. She knew [Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/) did not get along, and their side was suffering from it. This was the "price of anarchy", she thought — the amount that a group lost from its members independently pursuing their own separate goals without coordinating. She watched intently. The next minute, she knew, would determine if they could figure it out.

Watching from his hand device kilometers away, [Fin](/ˈfɪn/) felt his own frustration. [Zei](/ˈzA/) wanted to win, [Fin](/ˈfɪn/) knew, but almost as much, [Zei](/ˈzA/) wanted to hear [Bai](/ˈbI/) beg.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) stared at the board, concentrating his mind and trying to figure out his next move. After what seemed like an eternity, he decided to change his tactics.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) continued the attack on Dza, but intentionally did not target any of his symbols. Instead, he attacked a northern part of the eastern edge of Pan's territory, and spent a whole intervention turn to put up walls and build glider factories there. He put up more walls, just to let the gliders build up and bounce back and forth.

Pan and Dza did not see any of this. Instead, they saw [Zei](/ˈzA/) having greatly wounded Dza, but still struggling to finish him off, while Pan cornered [Bai](/ˈbI/) more and more toward the southeast. Emboldened, Pan launched an attack toward the east, seeking to sow chaos in the weakly defended territory in between [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s home base and the front in the northeast against Dza.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) saw that [Bai](/ˈbI/) was struggling. But the communication line between the two remained silent. She was still too proud to beg.

Then, [Zei](/ˈzA/) saw that Pan was sending against [Zei](/ˈzA/) the same type of moving wall that [Zei](/ˈzA/) had used himself. He realized that he could not beat Pan alone. And so, he used his intervention turn to try a new strategy.

First, [Zei](/ˈzA/) sent some gliders to destroy Pan's symbols in the center of the field. Then came the real attack. [Zei](/ˈzA/), [Bai](/ˈbI/) and the audience saw a spaceship flying diagonally northwest, from [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s homebase, straight toward Pan's. With all of Pan's symbols cleared from the path, Pan and Dza were oblivious to this. What Pan saw was that his attack had successfully split [Bai](/ˈbI/) and [Zei](/ˈzA/), and pushed [Bai](/ˈbI/) back all the way to her home base, surrounded on all sides. Dza still had five symbols, miraculously holding on against the force of [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s primary attack.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) checked the clock. Sixty turns until the next intervention turn. His spaceship was almost at Pan's base.
Forty turns.
Finally, [Zei](/ˈzA/) said the first words that went across his team's audio channel in this entire game.
"[Bai](/ˈbI/), next intervention turn is your chance to shine."
Twenty turns.
[Zei](/ˈzA/)'s spaceship crashed against the remaining intact southern wall of Pan's home base. It briefly fluttered into chaotic shapes.
Then, seemingly miraculously, for one single turn, the chaos came together into a symbol.
[Bai](/ˈbI/)'s symbol.
[Zei](/ˈzA/) could hear a gasp — the second message that went across his team's audio channel in this game.

[Zei](/ˈzA/) used his intervention turn to remove his own wall. Dozens of gliders flew in all directions, simultaneously targeting all of Dza's remaining symbols from multiple angles. [Bai](/ˈbI/) struggled in her sandbox view, made a few attempts at copying [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s trick from over a thousand turns earlier. On her third try, she succeeded, and she repeated her moves live. The symbol was walled off, and gliders were flying in all directions.
Two hundred turns later, all of Dza's remaining symbols had been eliminated.

The map once more: the plus signs are gone. [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s circles hold the bottom right and a cluster in the northeast. Pan's triangles fill much of the north, west and center. [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s squares remain in the bottom left, with a single square now up in the northwest.

By total symbol count, it was fifteen to fifteen — exactly even. But now, Dza was out, and [Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/) could do twice as much together in their intervention turns as Pan could do alone in his.

Pan made a last-ditch effort to send new kinds of gliders to destroy everything he could in [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s home base. He copied [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s signature tactic, sending a spaceship to try to set up a symbol there. The plan partially succeeded. But the keystone, setting up the symbol, did not. [Zei](/ˈzA/) had already put up the countermeasures, and blocked the spaceship in its tracks.

Meanwhile, [Bai](/ˈbI/) and [Zei](/ˈzA/) continued to wreak havoc on Pan's territory, [Bai](/ˈbI/) attacking the west and [Zei](/ˈzA/) attacking the north and east. A thousand turns later, most of the game field had become a high-entropy wasteland. The main untarnished territories were [Bai](/ˈbI/)'s home base, a fraction of [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s home base, and [Zei](/ˈzA/)'s side of what had been the battle front against Dza. Total symbol count: [Zei](/ˈzA/) five, [Bai](/ˈbI/) five, and Pan four.
At that moment, Pan resigned.
The audience cheered.
Two elevators opened up in the waiting room, and [Zei](/ˈzA/) and [Bai](/ˈbI/) simultaneously stepped out. [Mu](/ˈmu/) was waiting for them.
"Congratulations, you two. Next stop is the semi-finals in fifteen days."
"I'm confused. Everything in this game was the same as before. What was the new rule?"
"Ah. I thought you would ask that."
